title: Omnichannel Marketing in 2027: Strategies, Trends and Best Practices
summary: Dive in to learn about omnichannel strategies, how consumers are shopping today, and strategies to implement.
body_markdown:
Consumers don’t follow a straight path to purchase. They might discover a product on social media, research it on Google, compare prices on a retailer’s website, see an ad on Connected TV and eventually make a purchase in-store.


For marketers, the challenge isn’t simply being present across multiple channels. It’s making those interactions feel connected while reaching the right audiences with relevant messages.


That’s where omnichannel marketing comes in.


In this guide, we’ll explore what omnichannel marketing means in 2027, how consumer shopping behaviors are changing and the strategies marketers can use to create more connected customer experiences.


## What Is Omnichannel Marketing?


Omnichannel marketing is a strategy that connects customer interactions across multiple channels to create a more consistent and relevant brand experience.


Unlike multichannel marketing, where brands may use several channels independently, omnichannel marketing focuses on making those channels work together.


For example, a consumer might browse products on a retailer’s website, receive a relevant email, encounter a Connected TV ad and later visit a physical store. An effective omnichannel strategy uses available customer data and engagement signals to make these experiences more coordinated.


The goal isn’t to deliver the same message everywhere. It’s to deliver the right message through the right channel based on where consumers are in their purchasing journey.


## Omnichannel Shopping Trends in 2027


Today’s consumers have more ways to discover, research and purchase products than ever before. Search engines, social media, retail websites, streaming platforms, email and physical stores all influence purchasing decisions.


Several trends are shaping omnichannel marketing strategies.


### 1. Shopping Journeys Are Becoming Less Predictable


Consumers frequently move between channels before making a purchase.


A shopper might research a product online but purchase it in-store. Another may discover a brand through social media, compare alternatives on multiple websites and complete the purchase days or weeks later.


These journeys create opportunities for marketers to connect with consumers at different stages of consideration.


Rather than relying on a single channel, brands need to understand how different touchpoints contribute to awareness, engagement and conversions.


### 2. Consumer Intent Matters More Than Ever


Knowing who your customers are is important, but understanding what they’re interested in right now can make targeting more relevant.


Consumer intent data helps marketers identify signals that indicate what households may be researching or considering.


For example, a consumer researching home improvement projects may be a relevant audience for home furnishings, appliances or home services.


[PGM’s consumer intent signals](https://porchgroupmedia.com/online-audiences/) help marketers identify audiences based on observed research activity, creating opportunities to align messaging with changing consumer interests.


### 3. First-Party Data Is Central to Omnichannel Marketing


Customer data is one of a brand’s most valuable marketing assets.


Purchase histories, customer preferences, loyalty program participation and website interactions can provide useful insights into existing customer relationships.


However, many organizations struggle with incomplete, outdated or disconnected customer records.


Data hygiene, identity matching and data enhancement can help brands create a more useful foundation for segmentation and campaign activation.


### 4. Traditional and Digital Channels Work Better Together


Omnichannel marketing isn’t limited to digital advertising.


Direct mail, Connected TV, email, paid search, social media and in-store experiences can each play a role in reaching consumers.


The opportunity is to use audience intelligence to determine which channels make sense for different customer segments and coordinate messaging across those channels.


## Omnichannel Marketing vs. Multichannel Marketing: What’s the Difference?


Although the terms are sometimes used interchangeably, omnichannel and multichannel marketing are not the same.


**Multichannel marketing** involves reaching consumers through several channels, such as email, social media, direct mail and paid advertising. Each channel may operate independently, with separate campaigns, data and measurement.


**Omnichannel marketing** connects those channels to create a more coordinated customer experience. Audience insights, customer information and campaign engagement help inform how and when brands communicate across touchpoints.


For example, a multichannel retailer might send the same promotional message through email, social media and direct mail.


An omnichannel retailer might instead use customer purchase history, browsing behavior and audience insights to determine which message and channel are most relevant to each segment.


The difference is coordination, not simply the number of channels used.


## 6 Omnichannel Marketing Strategies to Reach Today’s Consumers


### 1. Build a More Complete View of Your Customers


A successful omnichannel strategy starts with understanding your audience.


Many brands have valuable first-party customer data but lack the additional information needed to create meaningful audience segments.


Data enhancement can help fill those gaps.


[PGM’s People Factors](https://porchgroupmedia.com/consumer-data/) data provides demographic, household and lifestyle attributes that can help marketers better understand their customers and develop more relevant audiences.


Combining these insights with existing customer information can support more informed segmentation and targeting decisions.


### 2. Use Consumer Intent to Improve Campaign Timing


Reaching the right audience matters, but timing can be just as important.


Consumers may begin researching purchases long before they’re ready to buy. Their interests can also change based on seasonality, household needs and life events.


Intent signals can help marketers recognize these shifts and identify audiences showing interest in relevant products or services.


For example, brands can use shopping intent trends to inform seasonal campaign planning, identify emerging category interest and refine their audience targeting.


### 3. Connect Digital and Offline Marketing Channels


Digital advertising may capture attention, but offline channels can reinforce awareness and encourage action.


Consider how different channels can support one another:


- **Email marketing:** Reach customers with relevant offers, product recommendations and retention communications.
- **Social media:** Build awareness, encourage engagement and introduce consumers to new products.
- **Connected TV:** Reach audiences through streaming environments using eligible audience targeting capabilities.
- **Direct mail:** Deliver tangible messages that can complement digital campaigns.
- **Paid search:** Connect with consumers actively researching products and services.
- **In-store experiences:** Reinforce brand messaging and create opportunities for purchase and customer engagement.


The key is to coordinate these channels around your audience and campaign objectives rather than treating each one as a separate marketing effort.


### 4. Make Data Quality a Priority


Even the best omnichannel strategy can struggle when customer data is inaccurate or incomplete.


Duplicate records, outdated contact information and missing customer attributes can make it harder to build reliable audiences and coordinate marketing across channels.


Regular data maintenance should include:


- Identifying and removing duplicate customer records.
- Standardizing names, addresses and other customer information.
- Updating outdated contact details.
- Enhancing records with relevant audience attributes.
- Reviewing identity matching and data activation requirements.

### 5. Personalize Based on More Than Demographics


Age, income and location can provide a starting point for audience segmentation, but they don’t tell the whole story.


Two consumers with similar demographic profiles may have very different interests, shopping behaviors and purchasing priorities.


Combining demographic and household information with lifestyle attributes and intent signals can help marketers develop more relevant audience segments.


For example, a home improvement retailer might segment audiences based on homeownership, property characteristics and interest in renovation projects rather than relying on age or income alone.


This approach can help brands develop messaging that better reflects consumers’ needs and interests.


### 6. Measure Performance Across Channels


One of the biggest challenges in omnichannel marketing is understanding how different channels contribute to results.


A consumer may see several ads, receive an email and visit a website before purchasing. Looking only at the final interaction can overlook the influence of earlier touchpoints.


Marketers should establish consistent campaign goals and measurement frameworks across channels.


Important metrics may include:


- Audience reach and frequency
- Engagement rates
- Website visits and conversions
- Customer acquisition cost
- Return on advertising spend
- Customer retention and repeat purchases
- Incremental sales or conversions, where measurable


Rather than measuring every channel in isolation, look for opportunities to understand how coordinated campaigns contribute to overall business outcomes.

## How to Build an Omnichannel Marketing Strategy


Getting started doesn’t require launching campaigns across every available channel.


Instead, focus on building a coordinated strategy around your customers and business goals.


**Step 1: Understand Your Audience**


Review your existing customer data and identify gaps in your understanding of customer characteristics, preferences and purchasing behaviors.


**Step 2: Identify Priority Segments**


Use customer insights, audience attributes and relevant intent signals to determine which audiences are most valuable for your campaign objectives.


**Step 3: Map the Customer Journey**


Consider how consumers discover, research and purchase your products. Identify the channels and touchpoints that may influence their decisions.


**Step 4: Select the Right Channels**


Choose channels based on audience behavior, campaign objectives and available resources. You don’t need to be everywhere to build an effective omnichannel strategy.


**Step 5: Coordinate Messaging**


Develop messaging that reflects the audience’s needs and stage in the purchasing journey. Keep your brand experience consistent while adapting content to each channel.


**Step 6: Measure and Optimize**


Monitor campaign results, compare performance across channels and use what you learn to refine your audiences, messaging and marketing investments.


## Frequently Asked Questions About Omnichannel Marketing


### What is an example of omnichannel marketing?


A retailer might use customer purchase history to identify relevant audiences, deliver personalized email offers, reach those audiences through eligible digital advertising channels and reinforce the campaign with direct mail. Each channel supports a coordinated customer experience.


### Why is omnichannel marketing important?


Consumers interact with brands across multiple devices and channels. Omnichannel marketing helps businesses coordinate those interactions, create more consistent experiences and develop more relevant campaigns.


### What is the difference between omnichannel and multichannel marketing?


Multichannel marketing uses several channels to reach consumers, often independently. Omnichannel marketing connects those channels through coordinated messaging, audience insights and customer experiences.


### How does customer data improve omnichannel marketing?


Customer data helps marketers understand who their audiences are, how they interact with a brand and what may be relevant to them. Data enhancement and audience intelligence can provide additional insights to support segmentation and targeting.


### What channels are used in omnichannel marketing?


Common channels include email, social media, paid search, Connected TV, direct mail, websites, mobile apps and physical stores. The right combination depends on the audience and campaign objectives.


### How do you measure omnichannel marketing success?


Marketers can evaluate reach, engagement, conversions, customer acquisition costs, retention and incremental business results. Consistent measurement across channels helps provide a more complete view of campaign performance.
